title: What We Carry Forward
author: Jonathan Boymal
summary: Boymal argues that the real test of teaching is whether students can carry what they learn into unfamiliar settings, and that this transfer can be designed for. He draws on cognitive science: varying contexts and examples builds overlapping memory pathways, depth over breadth supports consolidation, and spacing, reflection and sleep let the brain reorganise knowledge for flexible use. He adds Immordino-Yang's point that meaning and emotion bind cognition and identity together. He then moves to a philosophical frame, linking transfer to the Greek idea of phronesis, or practical wisdom. Generative AI can map structural analogies across domains, but human analogies are tied to memory and identity. His conclusion is that transfer is a moral and creative act, a decision about what to carry forward.
points: Teaching ideas across varied contexts and multiple examples makes later retrieval in new situations more likely, because memory encodes the context as well as the concept.
A course that goes deep on a few core ideas and traces their implications supports the consolidation needed for long-term memory, which favours depth over coverage.
Practice over time, reflection and sleep let the brain replay and reconfigure learning, so they are conditions for transfer and not extras.
Boymal frames transfer as phronesis, acting with insight in unfamiliar settings, and contrasts it with AI that only rearranges patterns.
quotes: Educators are asked to do more than guide students through the material of a course. The deeper challenge is to help them carry what they learn into new and unfamiliar settings; into other subjects, into professional life, and into the shifting contexts of the wider world.

When ideas are introduced in a variety of contexts, students are more likely to recognise their relevance and call on them later. Neuroscience helps explain why: the brain encodes the concept itself and the context in which it was learned.
By varying the contexts, and by relating concepts to multiple examples, we encourage the brain to build overlapping pathways, making it easier to retrieve knowledge in new situations.
Depth matters too. A course that lingers with a few core ideas, tracing them into their wider implications, strengthens the neural consolidation needed for long-term memory.

Yet beneath all this lies a philosophical question: what does it mean to carry knowledge from one place to another? The Greeks spoke of phronesis, or practical wisdom, the capacity to act with insight when the setting is unfamiliar.
Yet human analogies reach beyond structure alone. Ours are tied to memory, experience, and identity. To draw a connection is also to ask: what matters enough to carry forward?

This is why transfer, for humans, is a moral and creative act. It is how we apply knowledge across the boundaries of subjects, but also how we stitch together the fragments of our own lives into something coherent.
